narrative:
The model predicts a 48% probability that you will leave this organization, which is nearly a one-in-two chance. Because of this, your promotion request has been denied—promoting someone who is likely to leave in the near future is not a sound investment.

Three factors carried the most weight. The first, and strongest, is that you have received other job opportunities while working here. Among employees the model expects to stay, only about one in four has received such offers. This strongly pushes toward leaving, because you already have alternatives.

The second most important factor worked in your favor. Your six to ten years of tenure at this organization suggests commitment and accumulated knowledge, and this pushed the prediction toward staying. About a third of employees predicted to stay share your length of service.

The third factor, your six to ten years of total experience, pushed back toward leaving. Among employees predicted to stay, half have only one to five years of experience overall. At your experience level, people often reach a career turning point and begin looking outward.

Together, these signals created a fragile balance, but the presence of outside offers tipped the decision. The organization should consider addressing your recognition, career path, and growth opportunities to reduce your risk of leaving. You, in turn, might reflect on whether your satisfaction here can improve, or whether an external move genuinely serves your long-term career.
